@p17-643
S: scx
D: A
T: Large file uploads fail in production but work locally. Why?
K: large file upload fails, 413 request entity too large, upload size limit, maxallowedcontentlength, request body too large, upload timeout
X: Large uploads usually hit a size limit or a timeout somewhere in the chain, and production has more layers than local development, each with its own limit.
X: Find where it fails: the status code and response tell a lot. A 413 Request Entity Too Large comes from a component rejecting the size; a 404.13 on IIS means request filtering's maxAllowedContentLength; a 502 or 504 suggests a timeout at a proxy; a connection reset suggests a component closing the connection.
X: Check each layer.
X: The CDN, WAF or API gateway: many have body size limits, like WAF inspection limits, or API Gateway's 10 MB payload limit.
X: The load balancer or reverse proxy: nginx's client_max_body_size defaults to 1 MB, a common surprise in Kubernetes ingress setups.

X: The better design for large files: don't send them through the API at all. The client asks the API for a pre-signed upload URL, uploads directly to S3 or Blob Storage, possibly in chunks with multipart upload so it can resume, and then the API processes the file asynchronously after an upload event. That avoids all these limits, keeps the API light, and handles unreliable networks.
@p17-644
S: scx
D: A
T: A large export times out for big customers or studies. How do you fix it?
K: export timeout, large report timeout, csv export slow, excel export large data, async export, export job
X: A synchronous export that builds the whole file inside an HTTP request works for small data and fails for large data, hitting request timeouts, memory limits or locking the database for a long time.
X: Quick improvements, if the export only slightly exceeds limits: stream the output directly to the response instead of building the whole file in memory, write rows as they're read with a forward-only reader, use AsNoTracking and select only needed columns, and fix slow queries. Streaming a CSV can handle very large data with low memory.
X: But for truly large exports, I change the design to asynchronous.
X: The user requests an export; the API validates the request and creates an export job, returning 202 Accepted with a job id. A background worker processes the job: it queries the data in pages, writes the file to blob storage, records progress, and marks the job complete. The user sees progress in the UI and gets a notification, or the page polls, and downloads the file through a short-lived signed URL. Files expire after a while.
X: Benefits: no HTTP timeouts, retry if the worker fails, controlled concurrency so ten simultaneous big exports don't overload the database, and the option to run heavy queries against a read replica.
X: Also consider whether the export is really the need. Sometimes users export everything to filter it in Excel, and better filters or a report in the app serve them better.
X: In a regulated context, exports of sensitive data are logged with who exported what.

T: ECS tasks pass health checks normally but fail under load. What do you look at?

X: When tasks get marked unhealthy only under load, the health check endpoint is usually suffering from the same resource exhaustion as the rest of the app, and killing tasks under load makes things worse, because the remaining tasks take even more traffic. It becomes a death spiral.
X: What I check.
X: Is the health endpoint cheap? @p17-653
S: scx
D: A
T: Kafka consumer lag keeps growing. What do you do?
K: kafka consumer lag growing, kafka lag, consumer cannot keep up, kafka backlog, slow kafka consumer
X: Growing lag means consumers process messages more slowly than they're produced. I find out which side changed and where the time goes.
X: Look at lag per partition, not just total. If lag is high on all partitions, consumers are generally too slow or producers sped up. If it's concentrated on one or two partitions, it's a hot partition, where a popular key sends most messages to one partition, or one consumer instance is stuck.
X: Check consumer health: are all consumers in the group active, or did some crash, leaving fewer consumers than partitions? Are there frequent rebalances, visible in logs, which pause consumption each time? Rebalance storms happen when processing takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, so the broker thinks the consumer died.
X: Check processing time: what does each message wait on? Usually a database write or an external API call. Traces and timing metrics per message show it.
X: Fixes.
X: Scale out consumers, up to the number of partitions; beyond that, extra consumers sit idle, so more partitions may be needed for future growth.
X: Speed up processing: batch database writes, process messages concurrently within a partition where ordering per key allows, and cache lookups.
X: Fix hot keys by choosing a better partition key.
X: Tune polling: smaller batches or a longer max poll interval if processing is slow, to stop rebalances, and cooperative rebalancing to reduce pauses.
X: Then alert on lag and its growth rate, since lag translates directly into how stale downstream data is.
@p17-654
S: scx
D: A
T: DynamoDB throttles during a big batch import. How do you handle it?
K: dynamodb batch import throttling, bulk load dynamodb, batchwriteitem throttled, dynamodb import s3, unprocessed items
X: A batch import writes much faster than normal traffic, so it hits either the table's capacity or a hot partition, and normal user traffic gets throttled too.
X: Immediate fixes: slow the import down. Throttle the writer to a rate the table can take, with retries and exponential backoff with jitter. BatchWriteItem returns UnprocessedItems when throttled; the code must retry those, otherwise data is silently lost, which is a classic bug.
X: Look at key distribution: if the import data is sorted by partition key, like all items for one customer together, writes hit one partition at a time. Shuffling the order spreads the load across partitions.
X: Capacity: for a one-off import into a provisioned table, temporarily raise write capacity or switch to on-demand for the import, then switch back. Keep in mind that on-demand also has a ramp-up behaviour for brand new peaks.
X: Better approaches for large loads: DynamoDB's import from S3 feature loads CSV, JSON or Ion files into a new table without consuming write capacity, which is ideal for initial loads. For ongoing large imports, put the data on a queue and have consumers write at a controlled rate, which also protects user traffic.
X: Also check secondary indexes: each write to the table also writes to its GSIs, and if a GSI is under-provisioned, it throttles the base table writes too.
X: Afterwards, monitor throttled requests and consumed capacity per table and index.

X: For important emails, I also design for failure: track send status per message, retry transient failures, show users important information in the app rather than only by email, and monitor bounce and complaint rates.
X: In clinical systems, sites may depend on emails for important notifications, so delivery issues get treated as functional failures, not cosmetic ones.

T: An IIS app pool keeps recycling during the day. How do you investigate?

X: Crashes: an unhandled exception on a background thread, a stack overflow or an access violation kills the worker process, and rapid-fail protection may then stop the app pool entirely after several crashes. The Application event log shows .NET runtime errors and Windows Error Reporting entries.
X: Idle timeout: the pool shuts down after inactivity, which is a different symptom: slow first request.
X: For crashes, I configure ProcDump or DebugDiag to capture a crash dump, then analyse it to find the exception and stack trace, fix the bug, and verify the recycle events stop.

@p17-665
S: scx
D: A
T: An old ASP.NET app hangs under load with low CPU. What is happening?
K: aspnet hangs low cpu, sync over async deadlock, result wait deadlock, requests stuck legacy aspnet, thread pool blocked
X: High latency with low CPU means threads are waiting, not working. In older ASP.NET apps on .NET Framework, two causes are very common.
X: Sync over async: code calls .Result or .Wait() on a Task, for example to call an async HttpClient method from a synchronous controller. In classic ASP.NET, there's a synchronisation context that allows only one thread at a time per request; the async method tries to continue on that context while the request thread is blocked waiting for it, so it deadlocks, and the request hangs forever. Under load, even without full deadlocks, blocking threads drains the thread pool, and new requests queue up.
X: Thread pool starvation: many requests block threads on slow I/O, like synchronous database calls or HTTP calls, and the thread pool grows slowly, adding threads gradually, so requests wait in queues.
X: How to confirm: take a memory dump during the hang and look at thread stacks with DebugDiag or WinDbg. Many threads waiting in Task.Wait, Result, or Monitor.Enter, or in synchronous network calls, show the pattern. Performance counters show requests queued rising while CPU stays low.
X: Fixes: make the call chain async all the way, from the controller down, instead of blocking. If that's not immediately possible, ConfigureAwait(false) in library code avoids the context deadlock, but still blocks threads. Add timeouts to every outbound call. Raising minimum threads is a temporary relief only.

S: scx
D: A
T: HttpClient calls start failing with socket exhaustion errors. How do you fix it?
K: socket exhaustion, httpclient per request, too many sockets time_wait, only one usage of each socket address, httpclientfactory fix
X: Errors like "Only one usage of each socket address is normally permitted" or connection failures under load, with thousands of connections in TIME_WAIT state, typically mean the app is creating a new HttpClient for every request.
X: Why it happens: each HttpClient instance has its own connection pool. Disposing it closes its connections, but the operating system keeps each closed socket in TIME_WAIT for a while, up to minutes. Under load, the app opens new sockets faster than old ones are released, and runs out of ephemeral ports. The using statement around HttpClient looks like good practice, but it's the cause here.
X: How to confirm: netstat shows many connections in TIME_WAIT to the same destination, and the code creates HttpClient per call.
X: Fixes: reuse connections. In ASP.NET Core, use IHttpClientFactory with typed or named clients, which pools and recycles the underlying handlers properly. Or use a single long-lived HttpClient, a static or singleton instance, with SocketsHttpHandler and PooledConnectionLifetime set, like two minutes, so connections are recycled periodically and DNS changes are picked up, which a plain static client would miss.
X: For .NET Framework, a shared static HttpClient plus ServicePointManager settings, like ConnectionLeaseTimeout, give similar behaviour.
X: Also check connection limits per server, and that responses are disposed or fully read, because unread response bodies can keep connections busy.

@p17-674
S: scx
D: A
T: A background job holds locks and blocks users. How do you fix it?
K: background job blocking users, long running batch locks, batch update blocking, job causes timeouts, chunked batch processing
X: When a background job updates many rows in one big transaction, it holds locks for its whole duration, and users trying to read or update those rows wait, time out, or deadlock.
X: Confirm: during the problem, sys.dm_exec_requests and blocking queries show the job's session as the head blocker, holding many locks, maybe escalated to a table lock.
X: Fixes.
X: Process in small batches: update or delete, say, 1,000 to 5,000 rows per transaction, commit, and continue. Each transaction is short, so locks are released quickly, and lock escalation, which happens around 5,000 locks, is avoided. The job also becomes restartable, tracking progress, and uses less transaction log.
X: Make sure batch queries use indexes, so each batch touches only its rows rather than scanning the table, which takes more locks.
X: Use read committed snapshot isolation, so readers aren't blocked by the job's writes, which removes most user-facing blocking for read-heavy screens.
X: Schedule it away from peak hours, and throttle between batches with a short delay if needed.
X: Avoid unnecessary work: only update rows whose values actually change, and do calculations before the transaction rather than inside it.
X: For very large changes, consider building the new data in a separate table and switching over, instead of updating in place.
X: Then monitor blocking and job duration, so regressions show up before users notice.
@p17-675
S: scx
D: A
T: An index maintenance job caused an outage. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
K: index rebuild outage, index maintenance blocking, rebuild index locks, online index rebuild, maintenance window issue
X: Index maintenance is meant to help performance, but done carelessly it can take locks, fill the transaction log and saturate I/O.
X: What usually goes wrong.
X: Offline rebuilds: on editions or settings without online operations, ALTER INDEX REBUILD takes a schema modification lock, blocking all access to the table for the duration. On a large table, that's minutes or hours of outage.
X: Log growth: rebuilding a big index generates a lot of transaction log, which can fill the log disk, especially if log backups don't run during the job, and in availability groups it can overwhelm replicas.
X: Running at the wrong time: overlapping with business hours in another region, or with batch jobs and backups.
X: Doing too much: rebuilding every index every night regardless of need, burning resources for little benefit.
X: Fixes.
X: Use online rebuilds, with WAIT_AT_LOW_PRIORITY so the rebuild yields to user queries, and resumable index operations, which can be paused and resumed.
X: Be selective: rebuild only fragmented indexes that matter, reorganise moderately fragmented ones, or skip; on modern SSD storage, fragmentation matters less than statistics. Updating statistics is often the more valuable part.
X: Use a proven maintenance solution, like Ola Hallengren's scripts, with thresholds and time limits.
X: Schedule it in a quiet window for every region, ensure log backups run frequently during maintenance, and monitor blocking and log usage while it runs.

T: Money values are off by a cent in some calculations. How do you fix it?
K: rounding error money, floating point currency, decimal vs double money, off by one cent, rounding mode, precision loss json
X: Off-by-a-cent errors almost always come from using floating point types for money, or from inconsistent rounding.
X: Floating point: double and float in C#, and number in JavaScript, are binary floating point, which can't represent many decimal fractions exactly. 0.1 plus 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3. Summing many values accumulates tiny errors that eventually show up as a cent difference. Fix: use decimal in C#, and DECIMAL or NUMERIC with fixed scale in SQL, never FLOAT or REAL for money.
X: Rounding rules: .NET's Math.Round uses banker's rounding by default, rounding 2.5 to 2, while business users and other systems may expect away-from-zero rounding, 2.5 to 3. Use MidpointRounding explicitly, and agree on the rule with the business.
X: When to round: rounding each line and then summing gives a different total than summing and then rounding. The business rules must define which one, like rounding per line item for invoices, and the code must do it consistently everywhere, including reports and exports.
X: Front end: JavaScript numbers can lose precision on very large values, and calculations in the browser can disagree with the server. Do authoritative calculations on the server, send money as strings or with known scale if precision matters, and only format on the client.
X: Currency: different currencies have different numbers of decimal places, so the scale comes from the currency.
X: Then add tests with known tricky values and compare totals across the system.

[For example, the protocol may allow a short delay of the randomisation visit, or a documented manual process.] Any manual action must be recorded with full details, so that when the system is back, the transactions are entered or reconciled, the audit trail is complete, and the randomisation list and drug supply records stay consistent. Because blinding and allocation integrity matter so much, manual steps are tightly controlled.
X: What engineering does to make this rare and short: high availability infrastructure, tested failover and backups, careful releases with rollback plans, and monitoring that detects problems before sites do.
X: After recovery, we verify that no transactions were lost or duplicated, especially those in flight when the outage started, and support any reconciliation.
X: In an interview I'd emphasise that we design with this patient-facing impact in mind.

@p17-685
S: scx
D: A
T: Performance degrades as a database grows over the years. What do you do?
K: database growing slow, data growth performance, archiving old data, partitioning large tables, long term database performance
X: Gradual slowdown with growth is predictable, so I treat it as capacity planning, not a surprise.
X: Measure: track table sizes, row counts, query durations and resource usage over time, so I know which tables and queries are growing and at what rate, and can predict when they'll hurt.
X: Typical fixes, roughly in order of effort.
X: Indexes and queries: queries written when tables were small often scan; with millions of rows, they need proper indexes, and queries should filter on indexed columns and return only needed data, with paging.
X: Archiving: move old, rarely accessed data, like closed records, old audit entries or historical logs, to archive tables or a separate archive database, while keeping it accessible for reporting or regulatory needs. Retention requirements decide what can move and what must stay.
X: Partitioning: for very large tables, like audit or transaction history, table partitioning by date makes maintenance and archiving efficient, with partition switching to move old data almost instantly. It helps queries only when they filter by the partition key.
X: Columnstore indexes for reporting over large historical data.
X: Separating workloads: move reporting and analytics to a replica or warehouse.
X: Hardware and configuration: more memory to keep the working set cached, faster storage, and database settings.
X: For a regulated system, archiving has to keep data complete, retrievable and auditable for the full retention period, so it's designed with quality and compliance input.

S: scx
D: A
T: The master database is becoming a bottleneck for all studies. What do you do?
K: master database bottleneck, shared database bottleneck, central database contention, multi tenant shared db hot, scaling shared database
X: In a database-per-study design, the master database often holds shared data, like users, permissions, study registry and global configuration, and every request across all studies may touch it. As the number of studies and users grows, it becomes a hotspot.
X: First, find out what load it carries: the top queries by frequency and cost from Query Store, and which applications and features issue them. Often a few lookups, executed on every request, dominate.
X: Fixes.
X: Caching: data like study configuration, user permissions and reference data changes rarely but is read constantly. Caching it in memory or Redis, with invalidation when it changes, can remove most of the load. This is usually the biggest win.
X: Query efficiency: fix the expensive queries with indexes and better access patterns, and avoid chatty patterns, like one query per study in a loop.
X: Read scaling: route read-only queries to a readable replica.
X: Reducing coupling: move data that's really study-specific out of the master into the study databases, and avoid cross-database queries from study databases to master in hot paths.
X: Splitting responsibilities: separate the master's different roles, like identity, configuration and job scheduling, into separate stores or services, so they scale independently.
X: Connection management: ensure applications use pooled connections and don't hold them open.
X: I'd also check the master's availability setup, because if everything depends on it, its outage is everyone's outage.

D: A
T: A partner's SFTP server rejects your connections after their upgrade. How do you troubleshoot?
K: sftp connection refused after upgrade, ssh key algorithm not supported, sftp negotiation failed, host key changed, cipher mismatch sftp
X: After a partner upgrades their SFTP server, connection failures are often about security algorithms, keys or network changes, so I check the connection log details carefully.
X: Enable verbose logging in the SFTP client: the handshake log shows exactly where it fails, like key exchange, host key verification, authentication or channel opening.
X: Common causes.
X: Algorithm mismatch: newer servers disable old algorithms, like ssh-rsa with SHA-1 signatures, older key exchange methods, or CBC ciphers. If our client library or configuration only offers those, negotiation fails with "no matching algorithm". Fix: update the client library and enable modern algorithms, like rsa-sha2-256 or ed25519 keys and curve25519 key exchange.
X: Host key changed: the upgrade generated a new host key, so our client, which pins the old fingerprint, refuses to connect, correctly, because it could be a man-in-the-middle attack. Fix: get the new fingerprint from the partner through a trusted channel, verify, and update our configuration.
X: Authentication: our public key wasn't migrated, or the server now requires a different key type, or password authentication was disabled.
X: Network: a new IP address or port, or their firewall only allows our old IP, or our egress IP changed.
X: Permissions: the folders or paths changed.
X: Because our SFTP component supports multiple client libraries behind one interface, if one library can't support the new algorithms, switching provider through configuration is an option, tested first.
X: Afterwards, agree with partners on advance notice of upgrades and a test endpoint.

T: Users report the app is slow, but only on Monday mornings. Why?

X: A recurring weekly pattern points to something that builds up over the weekend, or to load that peaks at that time.
X: Load pattern: Monday morning is often the busiest period, with everyone logging in, catching up on work from the weekend, and processing backlogs. X: Authentication: many users' tokens and sessions expired over the weekend, so the identity provider gets a login surge.

@p17-693
S: scx
D: A
T: A long-running user request ties up the server. How do you redesign it?
K: long running request, request takes minutes, move to background processing, async request reply, 202 accepted pattern
X: If a request takes minutes, like generating a large report, running a simulation, or importing a big file, keeping the HTTP request open causes timeouts at proxies and browsers, holds server resources, and fails badly if the connection drops.
X: The redesign is the asynchronous request-reply pattern.
X: The API validates the request quickly, creates a job record with a status like Pending, puts a message on a queue, and returns 202 Accepted with a job id and a status URL.
X: A background worker, a hosted service, a separate worker service or a function, picks up the message and does the work, updating the job's progress and status, and storing the result somewhere, like blob storage or a results table.
X: The client checks the status URL periodically, or receives a push notification through SignalR or email when it's done, then fetches the result.
X: Benefits: no request timeouts; work survives server restarts because it's queued; retries happen on failure; concurrency is controlled, so ten big jobs don't overload the database; and the UI can show progress and let users keep working.
X: Details to get right: idempotency, so a retried submission doesn't create duplicate jobs, using an idempotency key; authorisation on the status and result endpoints, so users only see their own jobs; cancellation support; cleanup of old results; and clear error states.
X: For moderately long operations, under a minute, simply optimising the work may be enough; for anything longer, this pattern is the reliable answer.

D: A
T: Your service depends on a legacy system that is very slow. How do you protect your users?
K: slow legacy dependency, protect from slow dependency, legacy system bottleneck, wrap slow service, cache legacy data
X: I can't always fix the legacy system, but I can stop its slowness from becoming my users' problem.
X: Measure first: which calls are slow, how slow, and how often my service calls it per user action. Sometimes the biggest issue is my side calling it too often.
X: Then apply protections.

X: Caching: if the data changes rarely, like reference data or configuration, cache it with a sensible TTL, so most requests never touch the legacy system.
X: Asynchronous integration: for writes or long operations, put requests on a queue and process them in the background at a pace the legacy system can handle, giving users an immediate acknowledgement.
X: Replicated read model: for frequently read data, keep a local copy synchronised through change data capture, events or scheduled sync, and serve reads from it. Users get fast responses, accepting a small delay in freshness.
X: Bulkheads: isolate calls to the legacy system in their own limited pool, so its slowness doesn't consume all of my service's resources.
X: Graceful degradation: show what's available, and clearly mark what couldn't be loaded, rather than failing the whole page.
X: Longer term, these protections often become the first step of a strangler fig migration, replacing the legacy system piece by piece.

T: Error rates rise only during deployments. How do you get to zero-downtime releases?

X: If errors spike every time we deploy, something in the release process interrupts in-flight work or sends traffic to instances that aren't ready.

@p17-698
S: msa
D: A
T: How would you keep a search index in sync with a SQL database?
K: elasticsearch sync sql, opensearch sync, search index synchronization, change data capture search, reindex search
X: Full-text search, faceting and fuzzy matching are much better in a search engine, like Elasticsearch, OpenSearch or Azure AI Search, than in SQL. But then the same data lives in two places, and the challenge is keeping the index in sync reliably.
X: Options, from simple to robust.
X: Dual writes from the application: after saving to SQL, also update the index. Simple, but if the index call fails after the database commit, they diverge, and there's no easy way to know. I avoid this as the only mechanism.
X: Events through an outbox: the service writes the change and an outbox record in the same transaction; a relay publishes the event; an indexer consumer updates the search index. Reliable, with retries, and the index catches up even after failures.
X: Change data capture: read the database's change stream, like SQL Server CDC or Debezium on the transaction log, and feed changes to the indexer. No application changes, and every change is captured, including ones made by scripts or other apps.
X: Periodic sync: an incremental job using a last-modified watermark, simpler but with more delay.
X: Whichever path, I design for drift: index documents carry a version or timestamp, so older updates don't overwrite newer ones; there's a full reindex capability, building a new index alongside and switching an alias atomically, for mapping changes or recovery; and a reconciliation check comparing counts or checksums.
X: Security trimming matters too: index the fields needed for permission filtering, like site or tenant, and always filter by them.
@p17-699
S: msa
D: A
T: How would you design a stock reservation system that never oversells?
K: inventory reservation design, prevent overselling, stock reservation, concurrent allocation, kit allocation design, reserve and confirm
X: The core problem is concurrency: two requests see one item left, and both take it. The design must make the check and the update atomic.
X: Data model: stock per location and item type with available and reserved quantities, or individual items, like kits with unique ids and statuses, which is the case in clinical supply.
X: Atomic reservation, with a few options.
X: Conditional update in the database: UPDATE stock SET available = available - 1 WHERE id = @id AND available >= 1, then check the affected row count. If zero, there was no stock. One statement, no race.
X: For individual items: select and lock one available item with UPDLOCK and READPAST hints, so concurrent requests skip each other's locked rows, then mark it reserved in the same transaction.
X: Optimistic concurrency with a row version, retrying on conflict.
X: Reserve, then confirm: a reservation has an expiry. If the process completes, like a dispensing confirmed, the reservation becomes final; if it's abandoned, a background job releases expired reservations, so stock isn't locked forever.
X: Idempotency: each request carries an idempotency key, so retries don't reserve twice.
X: Rules applied during selection: expiry dates, first-expiry-first-out, blinding constraints and the right item type for the patient's arm.
X: Scaling: partition by location, so contention is only between requests for the same site's stock, and keep transactions short.
X: And reconciliation jobs compare reservations with confirmed transactions, flagging anything stuck.
@p17-700
S: msa
D: A
T: How would you design a reminder and scheduling service, like visit reminders?
K: design reminder service, scheduled notifications design, visit reminder system, delayed jobs design, scheduler service design
X: Requirement: send reminders at the right time, like three days before a patient's visit window opens, reliably, once, and adapting when schedules change.
X: Data model: a scheduled_notifications table with the target, like subject and visit, the type, the due time in UTC, the status and a version. Reminders are created or updated whenever the visit schedule changes, like after a randomisation or a visit being recorded.
X: Triggering: a scheduler process polls for due items, using an index on due time and status, in small batches. Each item is claimed atomically, with an update that sets status to Processing where status is Pending, or SELECT with UPDLOCK and READPAST, so multiple scheduler instances can run without double sending. Alternatives include delayed messages, like Service Bus scheduled messages, SQS delay up to 15 minutes plus a store, or EventBridge Scheduler for individual schedules, but a table gives easy querying, cancellation and auditing.
X: Sending: the claimed item becomes a message on a queue to the notification service, which renders the template and sends via email or SMS, with retries and idempotency by notification id.
X: Changes and cancellations: if the visit is rescheduled, update the due time; if the subject withdraws, cancel pending reminders. A version check prevents sending a stale reminder.
X: Time zones: compute due times from the site's time zone, handling daylight saving changes.
X: Monitoring: overdue pending items are alerted, so a stuck scheduler is noticed quickly, which is the same kind of check our AlertWatchDog jobs perform.

D: A
T: How would you design a document and report generation service?
K: report generation service design, pdf generation service, document generation microservice, async report design, template rendering service
X: Reports and documents, like PDFs, Excel files or regulatory exports, are often slow, resource-heavy and occasionally fail, so they belong in a separate, asynchronous service.
X: Flow: the client requests a report with parameters. The API validates input and permissions, stores a job record, and returns 202 with a job id. A worker picks the job from a queue, gathers data through APIs or a read replica, renders the output with a template engine, like a Razor or HTML template converted to PDF, or a library for Excel, stores the file in blob storage, and marks the job complete. The client is notified or polls, then downloads through a short-lived signed URL.
X: Design points.
X: Templates are versioned separately from code, so report layouts can change through a controlled process, which matters for regulated documents.
X: Determinism: the same inputs and template version should produce the same document; record the template version, parameters and data timestamp in the job, for traceability.
X: Scaling: rendering is CPU and memory heavy, so workers scale independently on queue depth, with limits per user or tenant so one big request doesn't starve others.
X: Resilience: retries with idempotency, timeouts for very large reports, and clear error messages.
X: Security: authorisation checked again when the file is downloaded, files encrypted at rest, expiry and deletion of old files, and an audit record of who generated and downloaded what.
X: Caching: identical requests within a short time can reuse the previous result.
@p17-702
S: msa
D: A
T: How would you design reliable webhook delivery to many subscribers?
K: webhook delivery design, outgoing webhooks, webhook retries, webhook dispatcher, deliver events to customers
X: Outgoing webhooks push events to subscribers' URLs, and the main challenges are unreliable receivers, retries, ordering and security.
X: Flow: when an event happens, the service records it through an outbox. A dispatcher finds subscriptions matching the event type and creates a delivery record per subscriber, then queues the deliveries.
X: Delivery workers send HTTP POSTs with the event payload, an event id, a timestamp and an HMAC signature header, so receivers can verify authenticity and reject replays. Short timeouts, like ten seconds, so slow receivers don't tie up workers.
X: Retries: on failure or non-2xx response, retry with exponential backoff and jitter, over hours or days, like at 1 minute, 5, 30, 2 hours, and so on. After the final attempt, mark it failed and notify the subscriber. Receivers must deduplicate by event id, because retries mean at-least-once delivery.
X: Isolation: one subscriber being down mustn't delay others, so queues or concurrency limits are per subscriber. A circuit breaker per endpoint pauses deliveries to a dead endpoint and disables subscriptions that fail consistently.
X: Ordering: if order matters, deliver sequentially per subscriber and entity, or include a sequence number so receivers can order or ignore stale events.
X: Visibility: a delivery log per subscriber, with request, response code and timing, a replay function, and a test endpoint feature for subscribers.
X: Security: validate subscriber URLs against SSRF, require HTTPS, and support secret rotation with two valid signatures during rotation.
@p17-703
S: msa
D: A
T: GUIDs vs sequential ids vs Snowflake-style ids: how do you choose?
K: guid vs int id, sequential guid, snowflake id, distributed id generation, uuid v7, primary key choice
X: Id choice affects database performance, security and how distributed systems create records.
X: Auto-increment integers: small, fast, naturally ordered, great for clustered indexes. But the database generates them, so you only know the id after insert, merging data from several databases causes collisions, and exposing them in URLs reveals counts and makes guessing other records easy.
X: Random GUIDs, version 4: generated anywhere without coordination, globally unique, unguessable. But they're 16 bytes, and their randomness fragments clustered indexes in SQL Server, because inserts land all over the index, causing page splits and slower writes.
X: Sequential GUIDs: NEWSEQUENTIALID in SQL Server, or UUID version 7, which .NET 9 supports with Guid.CreateVersion7(). They embed a timestamp at the start, so values are roughly ordered, which keeps index inserts at the end like integers, while remaining globally unique and generated in the application. That's a good default for distributed systems now.
X: Snowflake-style ids: 64-bit integers combining a timestamp, a machine id and a sequence. Ordered, compact and generated without coordination, but they need machine ids assigned uniquely.
X: My approach: internal clustered keys can be integers or UUID v7; public identifiers in URLs should not be guessable, so either UUIDs or a separate public id; and authorisation checks never rely on ids being secret.
X: For business identifiers, like kit numbers or subject numbers, those follow their own business formats separately from technical keys.
@p17-704
S: msa
D: A
T: What is two-phase commit, and why do microservices avoid it?
K: two phase commit, 2pc, distributed transaction, xa transaction, msdtc, why not distributed transactions
X: Two-phase commit is a protocol for making a transaction atomic across several resources, like two databases, or a database and a message broker. A coordinator first asks every participant to prepare, meaning to promise they can commit; if all say yes, it tells everyone to commit; if anyone says no, everyone rolls back. In the .NET Framework world, MSDTC did this, often transparently with TransactionScope across connections.
X: Why microservices avoid it.
X: Availability: all participants must be up and responsive for the transaction to complete. If one service or database is slow or down, the whole operation waits or fails. Locks are held during the prepare phase, so a stuck coordinator can leave resources locked.
X: Coupling: services would need to share transaction infrastructure, which defeats independent deployment and technology choices. Many modern components, like HTTP APIs, Kafka or cloud services, don't support it at all.
X: Scalability: coordination round trips and held locks limit throughput.
X: Instead, microservices accept eventual consistency with patterns that give reliability without global locks: the outbox pattern, so a local database change and an event are recorded atomically; idempotent consumers; and sagas, a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions if a later step fails.
X: Where strong consistency really is required, the better answer is often to keep that data in one service and one database, so a normal local transaction does the job.
@p17-705
S: msa
D: A
T: What are leader election and consistent hashing used for?
K: leader election, consistent hashing, distributed coordination, single leader pattern, partition assignment, hash ring
X: Both solve coordination problems when several instances of a service run at once.
X: Leader election: sometimes exactly one instance must do a task, like run a scheduler, process a singleton queue, or coordinate others. Instances compete for a leadership lease; one wins and does the work, renewing the lease periodically; if it dies or stops renewing, another takes over after the lease expires. Implementations: a Kubernetes Lease object, which client libraries support; a distributed lock with expiry in Redis, a database row with an expiry timestamp, or sp_getapplock in SQL Server; or coordination services like ZooKeeper and etcd. Watch-outs: a paused leader, like during a long GC pause, may think it's still leader after its lease expired, so work should carry a fencing token, an increasing number that downstream systems check, to reject stale leaders.
X: Consistent hashing: distributes keys across a changing set of nodes. Nodes are placed on a hash ring, and each key goes to the next node clockwise. When a node is added or removed, only the keys near it move, instead of almost all keys, as happens with simple hash modulo N. Virtual nodes smooth the distribution. It's used in distributed caches, like Redis Cluster's slot model, which is a related idea, partitioned databases like Cassandra and DynamoDB, and load balancers with session affinity.
X: In application design, I usually use these through infrastructure rather than building them, but understanding them helps reason about failover and rebalancing.
@p17-706
S: msa
D: A
T: How do you evolve event schemas without breaking consumers?
K: event schema evolution, event versioning, schema registry, backward compatible events, breaking event change
X: Events outlive code: consumers may be deployed at different times, and stored events may be replayed months later. So event schemas need careful evolution.
X: Rules for compatible changes.
X: Adding optional fields is safe, provided consumers ignore unknown fields, which I make a standard: tolerant readers.
X: Removing or renaming fields, changing types or meanings is breaking. Instead, add a new field alongside the old one, populate both for a transition period, migrate consumers, and then remove the old one only when nobody uses it.
X: Never change the meaning of an existing field silently, like changing an amount from units to cents.
X: Versioning: include an event type and version in the envelope, like ShipmentDelivered v2. For a truly breaking change, publish a new version as a new event type, possibly both versions in parallel for a while, and let consumers migrate at their own pace.
X: Schema registry: with Kafka, a schema registry, using Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema, enforces compatibility rules at publish time, like backward or full compatibility, so an incompatible schema is rejected before it reaches consumers.
X: Contracts and tests: consumer-driven contract tests for messages catch breaking changes in the producer's pipeline.
X: Upcasting: for event-sourced systems, old event versions are converted to the current shape when read, so business logic handles only the latest version.
X: Documentation of events in a catalogue, like AsyncAPI, makes ownership and versions visible.
@p17-707
S: msa
D: A
T: What is hexagonal architecture, or ports and adapters?
K: hexagonal architecture, ports and adapters, onion architecture, clean architecture vs hexagonal, domain isolation
X: Hexagonal architecture, also called ports and adapters, puts the application's core logic in the middle, with no dependencies on technology, and connects everything else through ports and adapters.
X: Ports are interfaces defined by the core: incoming ports describe what the application can do, like an IAllocateKit use case; outgoing ports describe what it needs from the outside, like IKitRepository, IClock, or INotificationSender.
X: Adapters implement those ports for specific technologies. Driving adapters call into the application, like an ASP.NET Core controller, a message consumer, or a CLI command. Driven adapters are called by the application, like an EF Core repository, a RabbitMQ publisher or an SMTP sender.
X: The dependency rule: adapters depend on the core, never the other way round. The core doesn't know about HTTP, SQL or message brokers.
X: Benefits: business logic is testable with simple in-memory fakes for the outgoing ports; technology can change, like swapping a message broker, by writing a new adapter; and the same use case can be triggered from different entry points, an API, a queue or a scheduled job, without duplication.
X: Onion architecture and clean architecture are close relatives with the same core idea, differing mostly in how they name layers.
X: The risk is over-engineering: lots of interfaces and mapping for simple CRUD services. I apply it where there's meaningful business logic, and keep simple services simple.
X: Our newer APIs follow clean architecture, which is this idea in practice.
@p17-708
S: msa
D: A
T: How do you use change data capture to publish events from a legacy database?
K: change data capture events, debezium, cdc to kafka, publish events from database, legacy database events
X: When a legacy system writes directly to a database and can't be modified to publish events, change data capture lets other services react to its changes anyway.
X: How it works: CDC reads the database's transaction log, which records every committed insert, update and delete, and turns each change into an event. SQL Server has built-in CDC, which writes changes to change tables; Debezium is a popular open-source tool that reads logs from SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL and others, and publishes change events to Kafka, usually through Kafka Connect. Cloud services offer similar features.
X: Benefits: no changes to the legacy application; every change is captured, including those from scripts and other applications; ordering per row is preserved; and nothing is lost, because it reads committed data from the log.
X: Challenges.
X: Raw change events reflect table structure, not business meaning. An "UPDATE on table X" isn't a "ShipmentDelivered" event. So a translation step, sometimes called an event transformer, should turn low-level changes into meaningful domain events, otherwise consumers become coupled to the legacy schema.
X: Schema changes in the legacy database affect the event stream.
X: Initial snapshots of existing data and catching up after outages need care.
X: Operational overhead: running Kafka Connect, monitoring lag, and the impact on the database's log retention.
X: It's an excellent tool for strangler fig migrations, syncing data into new services while the legacy system remains the source of truth.
@p17-709
S: msa
D: A
T: How would you split a shared database during a monolith migration?
K: split shared database, database decomposition, extract data from monolith database, shared tables migration, data ownership migration
X: The database is usually the hardest part of breaking up a monolith, because many modules read and write the same tables, often with joins, triggers and stored procedures crossing boundaries.
X: The approach I'd follow, gradually.
X: Map data ownership: for each table, which module writes it and which read it. The goal is a single owner per table, with others getting the data through the owner's API or events.
X: Separate within the same database first: move the new service's tables into their own schema, give the service its own database user with access only to its schema, and replace cross-boundary joins and foreign keys with API calls or local copies. This reveals hidden dependencies cheaply, while the data is still in one place.
X: Handle shared reads: other modules that need the data get it through an API, or keep a read-only copy updated by events or change data capture.
X: Handle shared writes: route all writes for that data through the owning service. Where the monolith still writes directly, synchronise temporarily with CDC, while code is moved over.
X: Move to a separate database once the service no longer depends on cross-schema access, with a data migration and a cutover, possibly using dual writes with verification for a while.
X: Throughout: reconciliation checks between old and new, feature flags for switching paths, and the ability to roll back each step.
X: It's slow, but each step reduces coupling while keeping the system working.
@p17-710
S: msa
D: A
T: Batch processing vs stream processing: when do you use each?
K: batch vs stream processing, real time vs batch, etl vs streaming, kappa lambda architecture, when to use streaming
X: Batch processing handles data in large chunks at intervals, like a nightly job processing all of yesterday's transactions. Stream processing handles each event continuously as it arrives, within seconds.
X: Batch suits: reports and analytics where hourly or daily freshness is fine; heavy computations over complete datasets, like month-end reconciliation, billing or full recalculation of forecasts; data loads into warehouses; and simplicity, since batch jobs are easier to reason about, rerun and test, and can use cheap resources during quiet hours.
X: Streaming suits: things that need fast reactions, like alerts, fraud or anomaly detection, notifications and live dashboards; keeping derived data up to date, like search indexes or caches; and spreading load evenly instead of a big nightly spike.
X: Trade-offs of streaming: more complex, with ordering, late-arriving events, exactly-once concerns, state management for aggregations over windows, and more infrastructure, like Kafka, Kinesis, or stream processors like Flink or Kafka Streams.
X: Many systems combine them: a stream handles real-time needs, while batch jobs do periodic full recomputation and reconciliation to correct any drift. Modern tools blur the line, as micro-batching gives near-real-time results with batch simplicity.
X: My rule: start with the business's freshness requirement. If daily is genuinely fine, batch is simpler and cheaper. If people act on the data within minutes, it needs streaming or at least frequent incremental processing.
X: In supply management, for example, resupply checks can be frequent incremental jobs, while temperature excursion alerts need near-real-time handling.
@p17-711
S: msa
D: A
T: What is contract-first API design with OpenAPI?
K: contract first api, api first design, openapi design first, swagger contract, generate client from openapi
X: Contract-first means designing the API's contract, usually an OpenAPI document, before writing the implementation, and treating that document as the source of truth.
X: The process: the team writes or edits the OpenAPI spec, with paths, operations, request and response schemas, error formats, and examples. It's reviewed in a pull request with the consumers, like front-end developers, partner teams, or other services, who can comment on naming, shapes and error handling before any code exists. Mock servers generated from the spec, with tools like Prism, let consumers start building against realistic responses immediately, in parallel with the backend work.
X: Then code generation helps keep everything aligned: server stubs or interfaces from the spec, and typed clients for consumers, like TypeScript clients for the React front end or C# clients for other services, using tools like NSwag, Kiota or openapi-typescript. In CI, the implementation is validated against the spec, and a diff against the previous version flags breaking changes.
X: Benefits: better API design through early review, consistency across teams with shared style guides and linting with Spectral, parallel development, and fewer integration surprises.
X: The alternative, code-first, generates the spec from code, which is convenient for internal APIs with a single consumer. ASP.NET Core's built-in OpenAPI support in .NET 9 makes that easy too.
X: For public or partner APIs, I prefer contract-first, because the contract is the product.

T: What is a golden path or service template, and why do platform teams provide one?
K: golden path, service template, platform engineering, internal developer platform, backstage, paved road
X: A golden path, or paved road, is the recommended, well-supported way to build and run a service in an organisation. Instead of every team deciding how to set up logging, health checks, pipelines, containers and monitoring, a platform team provides a ready-made path that already does it right.
X: What it typically includes: a service template, like a dotnet new template or a repository template, with the project structure, OpenTelemetry, structured logging, health checks, configuration and secrets handling, authentication, error handling, a Dockerfile, and a test project already set up. X: The key is that it's a path, not a cage: teams can deviate when they have good reasons, but the easy way is the right way.

D: A
T: How do you handle a data deletion request across many microservices?
K: right to erasure microservices, gdpr delete across services, delete personal data distributed, data retention vs deletion, crypto shredding
X: When personal data must be deleted, for example under GDPR's right to erasure, the challenge in microservices is that the data is spread across many services, databases, caches, search indexes, logs, backups and event streams.
X: Approach.
X: Know where personal data lives: a data inventory listing which services store which personal data, maintained as part of service design.
X: Orchestrate deletion: a deletion request creates a workflow, often a saga, that publishes a "delete data for person X" command or event. Each service owning personal data handles it: deleting or anonymising the records, and confirming back. X: Event streams and backups: immutable logs and backups make physical deletion hard. Backups that can't be edited are kept for limited periods, with deleted data not restored into live systems.
X: Conflicting obligations: in clinical trials, regulations require keeping trial data for many years, which can override deletion requests, and clinical data is usually pseudonymised, with identities held by the sites, not in the IRT. The legal and privacy teams define what can be deleted versus retained, and the system implements those rules.
@p17-714
S: msa
D: A
T: How do you handle write conflicts in an active-active multi-region setup?
K: active active conflicts, multi region writes, last writer wins, conflict resolution, crdt, multi master replication
X: In active-active, both regions accept writes, and data replicates asynchronously between them. If the same record is changed in both regions before replication catches up, there's a conflict, and the system must decide what the final value is.
X: Strategies.
X: Avoid conflicts by design: route all writes for a given entity to one home region, like by tenant or customer, so each record has a single writer at a time, while reads happen anywhere. This gives most of the availability benefits with few conflicts, and is often the most practical choice.
X: Last writer wins: the update with the latest timestamp wins. Simple, and built into databases like DynamoDB global tables and Cosmos DB by default, but it silently loses the other update, and depends on clock accuracy. Acceptable for data where losing a concurrent change doesn't matter, like a user's preferences.
X: Merge logic: application-specific resolution, like merging non-overlapping field changes, or a custom resolver in Cosmos DB.
X: CRDTs, conflict-free replicated data types: data structures like counters, sets and maps designed so concurrent changes always merge to a consistent result, used for things like collaborative editing or distributed counters.
X: Record and escalate: keep both versions and flag the conflict for human resolution, appropriate for important business data.
X: For critical operations with strict invariants, like allocating a limited item, active-active writes are risky; a single primary region for those writes, with fast failover, is often safer.
@p17-715
S: msa
D: A
T: What is load shedding, and how do you implement it?
K: load shedding, admission control, shed load under overload, priority requests, graceful degradation overload
X: Load shedding means deliberately rejecting some requests when the system is overloaded, so it can keep serving the rest well. Without it, an overloaded service tries to handle everything, queues grow, every request becomes slow, timeouts cause client retries, and the system collapses for everyone.
X: How to implement it.
X: Concurrency limits: cap the number of requests processed at once, with a short queue; beyond that, return 503 or 429 immediately with Retry-After. ASP.NET Core's rate limiting middleware has a concurrency limiter for this, and Kestrel and IIS have connection and queue limits.
X: Queue time limits: if a request has waited too long to start, drop it, because the client has probably given up already. Processing it wastes capacity.
X: Prioritisation: not all requests are equal. Keep capacity for critical operations, like a patient randomisation or dispensing, and shed lower-priority work first, like reports, exports, bulk syncs and background refreshes. This can be done with separate limiters per endpoint class, or separate deployments for critical and non-critical traffic.
X: Adaptive limits: adjust the concurrency limit based on observed latency, growing when the system is healthy and shrinking when latency rises.
X: Client cooperation: clients should back off on 429 and 503, with exponential backoff and jitter, and not retry immediately.
X: Degradation: serve cached or simplified responses instead of full ones.
X: Load tests should show the system shedding load gracefully, not falling over.
@p17-716
S: msa
D: A
T: What are hedged requests, and how do they reduce tail latency?
K: hedged requests, tail latency, p99 latency reduction, speculative retry, backup requests
X: In distributed systems, a request often fans out to several backends, and the slowest one decides the total latency. Even if each backend is usually fast, occasional slow responses, from GC pauses, noisy neighbours or network hiccups, make the p99 latency much worse than the median. That's tail latency.
X: A hedged request sends the same request to a second replica if the first hasn't responded within a short delay, like the p95 latency of that call, and uses whichever response arrives first, cancelling the other. Because the delay is set at a high percentile, only a few percent of requests get hedged, so extra load is small, but the slow outliers are cut off.
X: Polly v8 has a hedging strategy, and the .NET resilience packages provide AddStandardHedgingHandler for HttpClient, which can also route the hedged request to a different endpoint.
X: When it's appropriate: read operations, or idempotent ones, because the request may execute twice. Never for non-idempotent writes without idempotency keys. And when the backend has multiple independent replicas, so the second attempt is likely to land somewhere healthier.
X: Risks: under overload, hedging adds load exactly when the system is struggling, so limit the number of hedged attempts and combine it with circuit breakers.
X: Other tail latency techniques: timeouts with fast fallbacks, reducing fan-out, caching, and fixing the cause of slow outliers, like GC pauses.

T: How would you design a kit allocation service for clinical supply?

X: At a visit, the system must assign the right kit to the patient: correct treatment, available at the site, not expired before the next visit, while keeping the blind and never double-assigning.

@p17-718
S: msa
D: A
T: When would you use a workflow engine like Temporal or Durable Functions instead of a hand-written saga?
K: workflow engine, temporal io, durable execution, orchestration engine vs custom saga, durable functions vs saga
X: A hand-written saga stores state in a table, reacts to messages, handles timeouts with scheduled jobs, and implements compensations. For a few simple flows, that's fine. But as workflows grow longer, with timers, human approvals, retries and branches, the custom state machine code becomes complex and fragile.
X: Durable execution engines, like Temporal, Azure Durable Functions, AWS Step Functions, or newer .NET options, take over the hard parts. You write the workflow as ordinary code, or a definition for Step Functions: call activity A, wait for an approval signal for up to three days, then call B, and on failure run compensation. The engine persists every step's result, so if the process crashes, the workflow resumes exactly where it was. Retries with backoff, timeouts, timers lasting days or months, and visibility into each running workflow come built in.
X: When it's worth it: long-running business processes spanning hours to weeks; workflows with many steps, waits and human interaction; complex compensation logic; and when visibility into each instance's state is valuable for support and audit.
X: Trade-offs: a new platform to run or pay for, a learning curve, constraints like deterministic workflow code that can't call random or the current time directly, and versioning running workflows when the code changes.
X: For a two-step flow, a simple outbox and consumer is enough. For something like a multi-day approval and transfer process, an engine saves a lot of code and bugs.
@p17-719
S: secx
D: A
T: What is the OAuth token exchange or on-behalf-of flow?
K: on behalf of flow, token exchange, obo flow, downstream api user context, delegated token microservices
X: When a user calls API A, and API A must call API B as that user, so B can apply the user's own permissions, simply forwarding the user's token is a problem: the token's audience is API A, so B should reject it, and forwarding broad tokens everywhere increases the damage if one service is compromised.
X: The on-behalf-of flow, in Entra ID, and the standard OAuth 2.0 token exchange, RFC 8693, supported by Keycloak and others, solve this. API A sends the incoming user token to the identity provider's token endpoint, authenticating as itself, and asks for a new token for API B. The identity provider checks that A is allowed to call B on behalf of users and issues a token with audience B, containing the user's identity, and often A's identity as the actor. A calls B with that token, and B validates it normally.
X: Benefits: each token is scoped to exactly one audience, so tokens can't be replayed against other services; downstream services see the real user and enforce their own authorisation; and the identity provider controls which services may delegate to which.
X: Alternatives: if B doesn't need the user's identity for authorisation, A can call B with its own client credentials token and pass the user id as context, with B trusting A. That's simpler but means B trusts A to have checked permissions.
X: I'd use token exchange when downstream authorisation depends on the user, and client credentials otherwise.
@p17-720
S: secx
D: A
T: How does mutual TLS work, and when would you use client certificates?
K: mutual tls, mtls, client certificate authentication, certificate based auth api, two way ssl
X: In normal TLS, only the server presents a certificate, so the client knows it's talking to the real server. In mutual TLS, the client also presents a certificate, so the server knows exactly which client is connecting, at the transport level, before any HTTP request is processed.
X: How it works: the server is configured to request client certificates and trusts a specific certificate authority. During the handshake, the client proves it holds the private key for its certificate. The server validates the certificate chain, expiry and revocation status, then maps the certificate, by thumbprint or subject, to a client identity. In ASP.NET Core, Kestrel's ClientCertificateMode and the certificate authentication handler do this; behind a load balancer or gateway that terminates TLS, the gateway validates the certificate and forwards details in a header, which the app must only trust from that gateway.
X: When I'd use it.
X: Service-to-service communication in a zero trust network, often automated through a service mesh, which issues and rotates certificates.
X: Partner and B2B integrations, where a partner system connects to our API: certificates are harder to steal and replay than API keys, and some industries require them.
X: Device authentication, like IoT devices or machines.
X: OAuth can also bind tokens to the client certificate, so a stolen token is useless without the private key.
X: The operational cost is certificate management: issuing, distributing, rotating before expiry, and revoking, so automation is essential.
@p17-721
S: secx
D: A
T: API keys vs OAuth client credentials for partner integrations: which do you choose?
K: api keys vs oauth, partner api authentication, client credentials flow, api key security, machine to machine auth
X: Both authenticate a system rather than a user, but they differ a lot in security properties.
X: API keys are simple static secrets sent with each request, usually in a header. They're easy for partners to use, which is why they're popular. But they're long-lived, sent on every call, so any leak, in logs, proxies or code, gives access until someone notices and rotates them; they carry no scopes or expiry by themselves, unless the server implements that; and rotation needs coordination.
X: OAuth 2.0 client credentials: the partner authenticates to the token endpoint with its client id and a secret, or better, a private key JWT or certificate, and receives a short-lived access token with specific scopes, which it sends to the API. The long-lived credential is only sent to the identity provider, not to every API; access tokens expire in minutes; scopes limit what the partner can do; and the identity provider centralises management, rotation and revocation.
X: My choice: for anything sensitive, like clinical or personal data, or write operations, OAuth client credentials, ideally with private key JWT or mTLS for client authentication. API keys are acceptable for low-risk, read-only or public-ish APIs, or as an additional identifier for rate limiting and analytics alongside OAuth.
X: If API keys are used, I store only hashes, support multiple active keys for rotation, scope them, log usage per key, and allow fast revocation.
@p17-722
S: secx
D: A
T: How do you prevent open redirect vulnerabilities?
K: open redirect, returnurl validation, unvalidated redirect, redirect after login security, localredirect aspnet core
X: An open redirect happens when an application takes a URL from user input, like a returnUrl parameter after login, and redirects to it without checking. Attackers send phishing links using our trusted domain: our-site.com/login?returnUrl=https://evil-site.com. The user sees our domain, logs in, and is sent to a fake page that might ask them to "log in again" and steal their credentials. In OAuth flows, open redirects can even leak authorisation codes or tokens.
X: Prevention.
X: Only allow local redirects: in ASP.NET Core, Url.IsLocalUrl(returnUrl) checks that a URL is relative to our site, and LocalRedirect() throws if it isn't, which is what the default login templates use. Be careful with tricky inputs like //evil.com or /\evil.com, which some naive checks treat as local; the built-in helpers handle these.
X: Allowlists: if redirects to other domains are needed, like between our own applications, compare against an explicit list of allowed hosts, not a substring match.
X: Indirect references: instead of passing a URL, pass an identifier, like a page key, that the server maps to a URL.
X: For OAuth and OpenID Connect: register exact redirect URIs in the identity provider, with no wildcards, so codes can only go to our own applications.
X: Front-end code too: SPAs that read a redirect parameter from the URL and assign window.location need the same validation.
X: It's a small fix with big phishing protection value.

S: secx
D: A
T: What is insecure deserialization, and how do you avoid it in .NET?
K: insecure deserialization, binaryformatter, typenamehandling, deserialization attack, json deserialization security
X: Insecure deserialisation happens when an application turns untrusted data into objects using a serialiser that lets the data choose which types to create. Attackers craft payloads that instantiate dangerous types, called gadgets, whose constructors or setters run code, leading to remote code execution.
X: In .NET, the classic dangers.
X: BinaryFormatter: fundamentally unsafe with untrusted data, and Microsoft has removed it from .NET 9. Same for NetDataContractSerializer, SoapFormatter, LosFormatter and ObjectStateFormatter used without protection. Legacy .NET Framework apps may still use them, for example in caches, session state, or ViewState with MAC validation disabled.
X: Newtonsoft.Json with TypeNameHandling set to Auto, Objects or All: the JSON includes a $type property, and the serialiser creates whatever type it names. That's exploitable. Keep TypeNameHandling at None, or if polymorphism is really needed, use a strict SerializationBinder that only allows specific known types.
X: How I avoid it: use System.Text.Json, which doesn't instantiate arbitrary types; for polymorphic JSON, use its explicit JsonDerivedType attributes, which only allow declared types. Deserialise into specific DTOs, never object or dynamic. Treat any data from outside, including cookies, message queues and caches shared with other systems, as untrusted. Sign or encrypt serialised data that round-trips through clients, using Data Protection.
X: Scanning tools and analyzers flag dangerous serialiser use, which helps find it in large legacy codebases.
@p17-724
S: secx
D: A
T: How do you prevent path traversal when handling file names?
K: path traversal, directory traversal, dot dot slash attack, file download vulnerability, safe file paths
X: Path traversal happens when user input is used to build a file path, and the attacker includes sequences like ../ to escape the intended folder. A download endpoint like /files?name=report.pdf becomes /files?name=../../web.config, and the server returns its own configuration, with connection strings. On upload, attackers might write files into executable locations.
X: Prevention.
X: Don't use user input as a path at all, where possible: store files with server-generated names, like a GUID, and keep the original name only as metadata in the database. The user requests a file by id, the server checks authorisation and looks up the stored path.
X: If names must be used, validate strictly: take only the file name part with Path.GetFileName, reject names with path separators, .., drive letters or invalid characters, and use an allowlist of characters and extensions.
X: Canonicalise and check containment: combine the base folder with the name, get the full path with Path.GetFullPath, and verify it still starts with the base folder's full path, with a trailing separator, before accessing the file. That catches encoded tricks and different separator styles.
X: Least privilege: the application's identity should only have access to the folders it needs, read-only where possible, so a traversal can't reach sensitive files.
X: Better still, store files in object storage, like S3 or Blob Storage, with keys generated by the server, which removes the file system from the equation.
X: Archives need care too: extracting zip files with entries named ../something, called Zip Slip, is the same bug.
@p17-725
S: secx
D: A
T: How do you prevent command injection?
K: command injection, os command injection, process start security, shell injection, run external process safely
X: Command injection happens when user input is included in an operating system command, and the input contains shell syntax, like ; rm -rf or && net user, which the shell executes. In .NET, it typically appears when code builds a command string for Process.Start with cmd.exe or bash, for example to run a conversion tool or a script with a file name from the user.
X: Prevention, in order of preference.
X: Avoid shelling out: use a library or API to do the job in-process, like an image library instead of calling a command-line tool.
X: If an external program is needed, don't use a shell. Start the executable directly with ProcessStartInfo, UseShellExecute false, and pass arguments through the ArgumentList collection, which passes each argument separately and handles quoting, so input can't break out into new commands. Never concatenate input into a single command string passed to cmd /c or bash -c.
X: Validate input strictly with an allowlist: if a parameter should be a file id or a known option, check it matches exactly, and map user choices to fixed values rather than passing raw input.
X: Watch for argument injection: even without a shell, input starting with a dash can be interpreted as an option by the target program; use -- to end options where supported, or validate.
X: Run the process with least privilege, a restricted account, a timeout, and in a sandbox or container where possible.
X: The same thinking applies to PowerShell scripts run from pipelines or automation: parameters, not string-built commands.

D: A
T: What is an XXE attack, and is .NET vulnerable to it?
K: xxe, xml external entity, xml parsing security, dtd processing, xmlreader secure settings, xml bomb
X: XML External Entity attacks exploit XML parsers that process DTDs, document type definitions. An attacker sends XML with an entity that refers to an external resource, like file:///c:/windows/win.ini or an internal URL. If the parser resolves it, the file's content ends up in the parsed document, which may be returned to the attacker, or the server makes requests to internal systems, which is server-side request forgery. A related attack, the billion laughs or XML bomb, uses nested entities to expand a tiny document into gigabytes, exhausting memory.
X: In .NET: modern .NET, and .NET Framework 4.5.2 and later, have safe defaults for most XML APIs: XmlReader prohibits DTD processing by default, and XmlDocument doesn't resolve external resources by default in newer framework versions. But older code, and explicit settings, can reintroduce risk: setting DtdProcessing to Parse, using an XmlUrlResolver, or old XmlTextReader usage on .NET Framework versions before 4.5.2.
X: What I do: parse untrusted XML with XmlReader.Create and settings with DtdProcessing.Prohibit and XmlResolver null, which also stops entity expansion; set limits like MaxCharactersFromEntities and MaxCharactersInDocument; and validate against an expected schema where relevant.
X: This matters in integrations that receive XML files from partners, like older clinical data exchanges or SOAP services, which are common in legacy systems. Security scanners and analyzers flag unsafe XML settings, so I fix any findings in legacy code.
@p17-727
S: secx
D: A
T: How do you encrypt sensitive data in SQL Server: TDE, Always Encrypted or column encryption?
K: tde vs always encrypted, sql server encryption at rest, column level encryption, always encrypted, encrypt pii database
X: SQL Server has several encryption options that protect against different threats.
X: Transparent Data Encryption, TDE, encrypts the database files, logs and backups at rest. It's transparent to applications and protects against someone stealing the disks or backup files. But anyone who can query the database, including DBAs and the application, sees plain data. It's a baseline, and usually on by default in cloud databases.
X: Always Encrypted encrypts specific columns in the client driver, so data is encrypted before it leaves the application and stays encrypted in the database, in memory on the server and in backups. The keys are held by the client, in Key Vault or a certificate store, not by SQL Server. So DBAs and anyone with database access can't read those columns. The trade-off is that the server can't operate on encrypted data: deterministic encryption allows equality lookups, randomised encryption allows nothing. Secure enclaves extend this to some range comparisons and pattern matching. It needs driver support and careful key management.
X: Cell-level encryption with ENCRYPTBYKEY uses keys inside SQL Server, which gives control but means the server and its administrators can decrypt.
X: Application-level encryption: the app encrypts fields itself, with envelope encryption using a key management service. Flexible and database-independent.
X: My choice: TDE everywhere, plus TLS in transit; Always Encrypted or application-level encryption for a few highly sensitive columns, like personal identifiers, where restricting access even from administrators is required.

T: How do you monitor security events and detect attacks in your applications?

X: Prevention isn't enough; we also need to notice attacks and misuse. That starts with the application logging the right security events.

X: Integrity: security logs must be protected from tampering, sent off the server quickly, with restricted access, and retained according to policy.
X: Testing: during penetration tests or simulated attacks, check that the expected alerts fired, because detection that's never tested often doesn't work.

T: What do you check in a security-focused code review?
K: security code review, secure code review checklist, review for vulnerabilities, security review pull request
X: Automated tools catch common patterns, but many real vulnerabilities are logic flaws that only a human reviewer sees. In a security-focused review, I go through a mental checklist.
X: Authorisation: does every new endpoint have the right authorisation attribute or policy? Does it check that the user can access this specific record, not just that they're logged in? Are tenant or site filters applied consistently?
X: Input handling: is all external input validated, with types, lengths and allowed values? Any SQL built with string concatenation, raw HTML rendering, file paths, redirects or commands built from input?
X: Data exposure: do responses return only what's needed, or whole entities with internal fields? Are sensitive values excluded from logs and error messages?
X: Secrets and configuration: any hardcoded credentials, keys or connection strings? Are new settings secure by default?
X: Authentication and sessions: token handling, expiry, cookie flags, and changes to the auth pipeline.
X: Cryptography: standard libraries, no home-made crypto, no weak algorithms, randomness from secure generators.
X: Error handling: no stack traces to users, and failures fail closed, denying access rather than allowing it.
X: Dependencies: new packages, their trustworthiness and versions.
X: Concurrency and business logic: can actions be repeated, raced or done out of order to gain an advantage, like double-submitting or skipping a step?
X: For high-risk changes, like authentication or payment-like flows, I ask for a second reviewer with security experience, and threat-model the feature.

T: How do you handle findings from a penetration test?
K: penetration test findings, pen test remediation, vulnerability remediation process, security findings triage, pentest report
X: A penetration test report usually contains findings rated by severity, like critical, high, medium, low and informational. Handling them well is about triage, fixing the root cause and proving the fix.
X: Triage: for each finding, confirm it's valid in our context, understand the real risk, considering exploitability, data exposure and existing controls, and agree on the severity with the security team. Sometimes the tester's rating is adjusted, with justification, but I'm careful not to downplay findings just to avoid work.

Often a central fix, like a shared authorisation filter or a security header middleware, solves a whole class.
X: Add tests: an automated test that reproduces each finding, so it doesn't come back.
X: Verify: ask the testers to retest, or verify internally with evidence, and record the closure.
X: Learn: look at patterns across findings, and feed them into coding guidelines, review checklists, training and automated scans.
X: Accepted risks, if any, are documented and approved by the right people, with review dates.
